I've drafted notes for every verse, but they draw on fewer sources than you asked for. My search budget ran out before I could reach several of the sites. There are no Lutheran sources, and nothing from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, catholic.com or oca.org. On the "Catholic" side I found only one descriptive encyclopedia entry. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. I couldn't fetch Gill or the verse-by-verse pages on biblehub.com. Most of the Pulpit, Ellicott, Calvin, Matthew Henry and Wesley material below comes from search snippets, not full pages I read.

# Joshua 9: Research Notes

## Part 1: The traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 1–2 (the kings unite)**
- Guzik says the kings had more and more reason to fear after Jericho and Ai, so they planned a head-on battle. He also suggests that hearing about Israel's first defeat at Ai showed them Israel could lose, which he counts as a further effect of Achan's sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- Utley says vv. 1–2 introduce all of chapters 9–12. He adds that "This united Canaanite army never came together to fight Israel." https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary
- Utley also explains "beyond the Jordan": in Joshua it can mean either the east bank or the west bank. He describes three regions in v. 1: the hill country, the lower foothills (the "Shephelah") and the coastal plain. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary
- Matthew Henry sees the kings' minds as blinded and their hearts hardened. He says Israel could learn from these usual rivals how to set aside quarrels and unite against God's enemies. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary
- Kenneth Mathews notes that "hear" runs through the chapter as a chain of reactions. The nations hear and plot an attack, the Gibeonites hear and plot surrender, and Israel hears and admits its oath can't be undone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary

**v. 3 (Gibeon hears)**
- Guzik quotes Trapp: the same news hardens some and makes others afraid. Gibeon chose a different strategy from the other kings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- Wiersbe says Gibeon achieved by deceit what Jericho's walls and Ai's weapons could not. He also notes that "it is usually after a great victory that Satan begins his subtle attacks." https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary
- Constable has a different angle. He reads Gibeon as having learned of Israel's own crafty methods at Jericho and Ai and deciding to use deception too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-9.html

**vv. 4–5 (the disguise)**
- Guzik says the Gibeonites were clever, misrepresented who they were and backed this up with false evidence. They wanted a treaty that Israel was forbidden to make with Canaanite peoples (Exod 23:31–33). He draws a lesson: things that only look old are not more trustworthy because of it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- Matthew Henry, quoting Bishop Hall, warns that God's people are often taken in by a show of age. errors are never the older for being patched. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_009.cfm
- A. W. Pink sees Satan here switching from open warfare to cunning, trying to slip his "leaven" into Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary
- Precept Austin points out that archaeology at el-Jib (ancient Gibeon) suggests winemaking was a major trade there, which fits the wineskins of v. 4. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary

**v. 6 (the request at Gilgal)**
- Several writers say the Gibeonites knew the law let Israel make peace with distant cities (Deut 20:10–15) but not with nearby ones. Their whole plan depended on looking distant. https://biblehub.com/q/How_did_Gibeonites_deceive_Israel.htm
- Gene Getz concludes from this that they used God's words to deceive Joshua. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary

**v. 7 (Israel's suspicion)**
- Guzik says Israel's men knew they couldn't make a treaty with Canaanites and even saw the risk, but they didn't take their skepticism far enough. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- Benson (a Methodist writer) takes "among us" to mean in the land, and so among the peoples Israel was forbidden to covenant with. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/9-7.html

**v. 8 ("We are your servants")**
- Madvig, quoted by Guzik, says the phrase offered vassal status. In return the Gibeonites expected protection, which they later called on in Joshua 10:6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- Precept Austin notes that they never actually answer Joshua's question about who they are and where they come from. They stay humble and avoid naming their people or home. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary
- Coffman calls their answer a mix of truth, falsehood, and hypocrisy. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/joshua-9.html

**vv. 9–10 (the fame of the LORD)**
- Ellicott says they deliberately mention only older events, Egypt and the two Amorite kings. They leave out the crossing of the Jordan, Jericho and Ai, because news of those could not yet have reached a truly distant land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-9.html
- Matthew Henry, from a separate snippet: one lie leads to another. Having claimed a far country once, they had to repeat it and then lie about their bread and clothes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/9-7.html

**v. 11 (sent by the elders)**
- Mattoon suggests Gibeon was governed by elders, not a king. Matthew Henry likewise notes that he can't recall a king of Gibeon being mentioned anywhere. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_009.cfm

**vv. 12–13 (the "proof")**
- One Bible Hub article treats the bread as a "time-stamp": physical evidence offered to answer the very question Israel was likely to ask. https://biblehub.com/q/How_did_Gibeonites_deceive_Israel.htm
- Coffman calls the claims about the bread, wineskins and clothes an outright falsehood. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/joshua-9.html
- Mattoon argues that thinking it through would have exposed the trick. A real embassy would have brought more supplies, a larger escort and fresh bread. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary

**v. 14 (they did not ask the LORD)**
- This is the key verse for almost every source. Guzik says the real problem was not the clever props but that Israel never asked the LORD. They trusted what they could see and touch, walking by sight, not faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- Constable says the writer plainly names the cause, linking it to Numbers 27:21 and James 4:2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-9.html
- The Pulpit Commentary calls this the same mistake Joshua made at Ai: he failed to consult God's appointed means of guidance both times. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joshua-9.html
- **What "took of their provisions" means is debated:**
  - Coffman thinks Israel shared a covenant meal, part of making the treaty. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/joshua-9.html
  - Ellicott, following the ancient Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum), prefers "they accepted the men on the strength of their provisions." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-9.html
  - Utley notes that the Hebrew text lacks "of Israel," so it is unclear who took the provisions. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary

**v. 15 (the treaty and oath)**
- Precept Austin explains the ancient practice of "cutting covenant," the most solemn and binding agreement of the day. It suggests, while admitting the text doesn't say so, that an animal may have been cut in two. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary
- Utley says an oath in the LORD's name was binding even when made under false pretences. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary

**vv. 16–17 (the truth comes out)**
- Guzik says marching to their cities was the proper test, but it came too late. Quoting Clarke, he notes that Kiriath-jearim later housed the ark for twenty years. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- Calvin sees God's paternal indulgence in Israel passing safely through the region. God pardoned their fault and turned it to their good. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/9-16.html

**v. 18 (the congregation grumbles)**
- Constable quotes a writer who says the wilderness pattern is reversed here. In the wilderness the leaders were in the right and the people at fault; here it is the other way round. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-9.html
- Madvig, quoted by Guzik, offers two possible reasons for the grumbling: lost plunder, or fear of another judgment like Ai. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- The Biblical Illustrator notes that the people grumbled but still submitted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/9-15.html

**vv. 19–20 (the oath must stand)**
- Guzik cites Psalm 15:4, keeping an oath even when it hurts. He says the leaders wisely refused to add a second sin to the first, and that breaking the oath would have been a sin against God more than against Gibeon. He connects this to Saul's later breach and the famine of 2 Samuel 21. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- Madvig, via Constable: since the oath was made in the LORD's name, fidelity was owed, not to the Gibeonites, but to the Lord. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-9.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: breaking the oath would have dishonoured God's name. Any fault in being deceived was Israel's own, because God had given them a way to detect the trick. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joshua-9.html
- Bush, quoted on Precept Austin, adds two points:
  - Joshua could have used a technicality, saying the treaty covered a "far country," not these nearby cities. He refused to.
  - Breaking it would have given God's enemies reason to blaspheme. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary
- Spurgeon: a Christian's word should be as binding as an oath. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary

**v. 21 (woodcutters and water carriers)**
- Constable: the punishment was designed to reduce the risk that the Gibeonites would draw Israel into idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-9.html
- Barnes says the same: the solution kept both the oath and the purpose behind God's command. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/9-22.html
- Guzik links the outcome to Deuteronomy 20:10–11, where a city that accepts peace is put under forced labour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/

**vv. 22–23 (Joshua's rebuke and curse)**
- Ellicott: Solomon appears to have followed this precedent with the remaining Canaanites (1 Kings 9:20–21). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-9.html
- The Pulpit Commentary goes further. It sees the Gibeonites' servitude as fulfilling Noah's curse on the descendants of Ham (Gen 9:25). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joshua-9.html
- Bible Hub compares the trick to Jacob's deception of Isaac and to Achan's sin in Joshua 7. https://biblehub.com/joshua/9-22.htm

**vv. 24–25 (Gibeon's explanation)**
- Coffman grants that their answer was honest but says it could not excuse the fraud. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/joshua-9.html
- Guzik: they made no complaint and accepted lowly service gladly. He compares their attitude to Psalm 84:10, "I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- Mathews, via Precept Austin, sees irony. The Gibeonites act on Moses' words more consistently than Israel does. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary

**v. 26 (delivered from death)**
- Coffman compares this to Cain, who was both punished and protected. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/joshua-9.html

**v. 27 (servants at the altar)**
- Precept Austin finds it striking that the deceivers end up serving before the LORD. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary
- The Biblical Illustrator traces some Gibeonites who rose in God's service: Ismaiah, one of David's mighty men, and Melatiah, who helped rebuild Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/9-7.html
- Bible Hub: by the time of the tabernacle and temple, Gibeon was close to the centre of worship (2 Chron 1:3). https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Gibeonites_trick_Joshua.htm

## Part 2: Where interpreters differ

The sources mostly split by individual writer, not by denomination. I found no Lutheran material. The only Wesleyan sources I found were Benson's note on v. 7 (in Part 1), Wesley's own one-line gloss on v. 7, and a Wesley note on 1 Kings 9.

**vv. 9, 24: Was the Gibeonites' faith real?**
- **Skeptical:** Constable says most commentators see them as enemies whose craftiness extended to their profession of the fear of Yahweh. He adds that Scripture never calls them converts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-9.html
- **Sympathetic (Calvary Chapel):** Guzik says that despite their lies they had a proper admiration and honor for the God of Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- **Sympathetic (Presbyterian, on a Baptist site):** Tyler Kenney, a Presbyterian pastor writing on desiringgod.org, hears real faith in v. 24. He argues it is not the "faith of demons" in James 2:19. He draws parallels with Rahab and sees God blessing the nations through Israel even when Israel is unaware. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/good-news-in-the-gibeonite-deception
- **A middle view (Pulpit Commentary):** their action mixed the good of a rudimentary faith, there is the evil of deceit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/joshua/9.htm
- **Matthew Henry** applies the story to repentance: make peace with God in the rags of humiliation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_009.cfm

**vv. 15, 19: Was the oath lawful, and why did it bind?**
- **Matthew Henry:** the oath was binding because it was lawful. He reads God's command charitably, as covering only those who refused to surrender. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/9-15.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Israel judged that an oath outweighs a command that isn't rooted in morality itself. It calls this a delicate point for moralists. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joshua-9.html
- **Wesley (Methodist)**, writing on 1 Kings 9 and pointing to the Gibeonites: the command to destroy the Canaanites was conditional, otherwise the oaths could not have bound Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-9.html
- **Clarke (Methodist), quoted by Guzik:** the command aimed at ending the Canaanites' political existence more than their lives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- **Barnes takes the opposite view:** the covenant was "unlawful," but Israel had to honour both the oath and God's intent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/9-22.html
- **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** God might have spared Gibeon anyway, as he spared Rahab, but Joshua and the princes still did wrong to swear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-9.html

**Who is to blame?**
- Gaebelein (Brethren) says the deceptions were inspired by the father of lies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/joshua-9.html
- The Biblical Illustrator adds that God allowed the trick partly to show mercy to the very chief of sinners. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/9-7.html

## Part 3: Other views (very limited)

- **Modern critical scholarship:** I found this only second-hand. Coffman reports, and rejects, Longacre's view that two versions of the story have been combined because two reasons for the treaty are given. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/joshua-9.html
- **Archaeology:** Precept Austin notes that el-Jib shows continuous occupation with no full destruction layer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-9-commentary Guzik, quoting Hess, says the site's identification seems assured from wine-jar handles stamped "Gibeon." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-9/
- **Catholic:** the only thing I found was the Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Beroth (Beeroth, v. 17). It simply retells the story and links Beeroth to Saul's later attack on the Gibeonites. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02515a.htm
